name: Ctesiphon
info: Ctesiphon was an ancient city on the eastern bank of the Tigris, south-east of present-day Baghdad, founded in the late 120s BCE and the royal capital of the Parthian and Sasanian empires for over eight hundred years.

facts.founded: In the late 120s BCE, on the site of a military camp that Mithridates I of Parthia had set up across the river from Seleucia.
facts.where: On the eastern bank of the Tigris, about 35 km south-east of Baghdad in present-day Iraq, at the place now called Al-Mada'in.
facts.known: Royal capital of the Parthians and the Sasanians; the metropolis called al-Mada'in, 'The Cities'; Roman attacks of the 2nd and 3rd centuries; seat of the patriarch of the Church of the East; the Arab conquest of 637; the Taq Kasra
facts.today: Ctesiphon is an archaeological site near the Iraqi town of Salman Pak, where the Taq Kasra, sometimes called the Arch of Ctesiphon, is the most conspicuous structure remaining.

t: Ctesiphon began in the late 120s BCE as a Parthian military camp across the Tigris from Seleucia, became the capital around 58 BCE and merged with Seleucia and nearby towns into a metropolis.
The Romans took it several times, three times in the 2nd century alone, and in 226 the Sasanians made it their capital and enlarged it.
The Arabs occupied it in early 637, and after the founding of Baghdad in the 760s it declined and was depopulated by the end of the 8th century.
dyk: In the late 6th and early 7th century Ctesiphon was listed as the largest city in the world by some accounts, and it measured 30 square kilometres, more than twice the 13.7 square kilometres of imperial Rome in the 4th century.
ev: Ctesiphon is founded on the site of a Parthian military camp
The city becomes the capital of the Parthian Empire under Orodes II
The emperor Trajan captures Ctesiphon, and Hadrian returns it in 117
Septimius Severus sacks the city and sells thousands of its people into slavery
The Sasanians hold Ctesiphon and make it their capital
After the conquest of Antioch, Khosrow I builds a new city near Ctesiphon for the people he captured
The founding of Baghdad draws away the city's political and economic life

sections.origins:
Ctesiphon stood on the eastern bank of the Tigris, across the river from the Hellenistic city of Seleucia. It was founded in the late 120s BCE, built on the site of a military camp established by Mithridates I of Parthia. In the geographer Strabo's account it was a large village, which the Parthian kings used as their winter residence so that the people of Seleucia would not be oppressed by having Scythian soldiery quartered among them. Strabo wrote that, because of Parthian power, Ctesiphon had become a city rather than a village, equipped with buildings and with wares and arts that pleased the Parthians. The kings spent the winter there for the healthy air and summered at Ecbatana and in Hyrcania.

The reign of Gotarzes I saw Ctesiphon reach a peak as a political and commercial centre, and the city became the capital of the empire around 58 BCE under Orodes II. The move west may have been due in part to the nearness of the earlier capitals, Mithradatkirt and Hecatompylos in Hyrcania, to Scythian incursions. Gradually the city merged with Seleucia and other nearby settlements to form a cosmopolitan metropolis.
sections.growth:
Ctesiphon was greatly enlarged and flourished under Sasanian rule, which began by 226, and it turned into a metropolis known in Arabic as al-Mada'in and in Aramaic as Mahoze. It developed into a rich commercial city, merging with the towns along both shores of the river, including Seleucia. Ctesiphon and its surroundings were therefore sometimes called 'The Cities'. The city measured 30 square kilometres, more than twice the 13.7 square kilometres of imperial Rome in the 4th century, and in the late 6th and early 7th century some accounts listed it as the largest city in the world.

After the conquest of Antioch in 541, Khosrow I built a new city near Ctesiphon for the inhabitants he captured and called it Veh-Antiok-Xusrō, which means 'village of Antioch Khosrow built this'. Local people called it Rumagan, 'town of the Romans', and the Arabs al-Rumiyya. After a campaign in 573, John of Ephesus wrote that no fewer than 292,000 people had been deported from Dara, Apamia and other Syrian towns to the new city, and later cited a letter giving no more than 30,000 prisoners. The first number is thought not to be meant literally. Khosrow built a number of other fortified cities along with it.
sections.rulers:
Ctesiphon belonged to the Parthian Empire from its founding, and the Parthian kings made it their capital around 58 BCE. By 226 it was in the hands of the Sasanian Empire, which also made it its capital and ended the Parthian dynasty of Iran. For over eight hundred years it served as a royal capital of the Iranian empires.

Rome took the city four or five times in its history, three times in the 2nd century alone. The emperor Trajan captured it in 116, and his successor Hadrian willingly returned it in 117 as part of a peace settlement. The general Avidius Cassius captured it in 164 during another Parthian war but abandoned it when peace was concluded. In 197 Septimius Severus sacked it. Under Sasanian rule Severus Alexander advanced on Ctesiphon in 233 and, as Herodian corroborates, his armies suffered a humiliating defeat against Ardashir I. The emperor Carus sacked the city uncontested in 283, during a period of civil upheaval. Some historians have claimed that Galerius captured it, but no source states this explicitly and scholars still debate it.

In 590 Bahram Chobin of the House of Mihran drove the newly ascended Khosrow II from Iraq, and a year later Khosrow, with Byzantine aid, reconquered his lands. In 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius surrounded the city and left after the Persians accepted his peace terms. In 629 the usurper Shahrbaraz held it briefly before his assassination, and the Pahlav and Parsig factions of the empire then fought constantly.
sections.life:
The city's population under the Sasanians was heavily mixed and included Arameans, Persians, Greeks and Assyrians. Several religions were practised there, among them Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism. Church councils of the Church of the East met at the city or at the Greek colony across the river in about 325 and again in 410, and in 497 the first East Syriac patriarch, Mar Babai I, fixed his see at Seleucia-Ctesiphon. Manichaeans, a dualist church, continued to be mentioned there under Umayyad rule and kept a patriarchate of Babylon in the city until the surviving Manichaeans fled in the ninth century and moved it to Samarkand.

The city was divided into districts. The oldest inhabited part lay on the eastern side, which Arabic sources call the Old City and where the Sasanian residence, the White Palace, stood. The southern side, Asbānbar, was known for its halls, riches, games, stables and baths, and the Taq Kasra stood there. The western side was Veh-Ardashir, 'the good city of Ardashir', which Jews called Mahoza, Christians Kokhe and Arabs Behrasir. It was populated by many wealthy Jews and was the seat of the Nestorian patriarch's church. Further districts included Valashabad, Hanbu Shapur, Darzanidan, Veh Jondiu-Khosrow, Nawinabad and Kardakadh.
sections.crises:
Ctesiphon's strategic importance made it a military objective of the Roman emperors in their eastern wars, and it was sacked more than once. Septimius Severus sacked it in 197 and carried off thousands of its inhabitants, whom he sold into slavery. Carus sacked it in 283. The Battle of Ctesiphon was fought in 363.

Under Khosrow II some of the fame of al-Mada'in faded because of the popularity of his new winter residence, Dastagerd. In 628 a deadly plague struck Ctesiphon, al-Mada'in and the rest of the western part of the Sasanian Empire, and it killed Khosrow's son and successor Kavad II.

In the mid-630s the Arabs defeated the Sasanians at the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah and then attacked Ctesiphon, which they occupied in early 637. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas quickly seized Valashabad and made a treaty with the people of Veh-Antiok-Xusrō and Veh-Ardashir: those of the former could leave or acknowledge Muslim authority and pay the jizya. The Muslims found Ctesiphon completely desolated, because the Sasanian royal family, nobles and troops had fled. They took some troops captive and seized many riches from the royal treasury, and the throne hall of the Taq Kasra was briefly used as a mosque. Much of the population fled after the capture.
sections.legacy:
Political and economic fortune passed elsewhere, and the city went into rapid decline, especially after the Abbasid capital Baghdad was founded in the 760s. Ctesiphon soon became a ghost town and was depopulated by the end of the 8th century. The caliph al-Mansur took much of the material needed to build Baghdad from its ruins. He also tried to demolish the palace and reuse its bricks for his own palace but gave up when the undertaking proved too vast. He used the town of al-Rumiya as the Abbasid capital for a few months. Ctesiphon is believed to be the basis for the city of Isbanir in One Thousand and One Nights.

In November 1915 the ruins were the site of a major battle of the First World War, in which the Ottoman Empire defeated British troops attempting to capture Baghdad and drove them back some 40 miles before trapping the force and compelling it to surrender.

A German Oriental Society expedition under Oscar Reuther excavated in 1928 and 1929, and a joint expedition of the Berlin State Museums and the Metropolitan Museum of Art worked there in 1931 and 1932. An Italian team from the University of Turin worked in the late 1960s and early 1970s on the far side of the Tigris, at Veh Ardashir. The Taq Kasra, once part of the royal palace, is estimated to date between the 3rd and 6th centuries and stands in the Iraqi town of Salman Pak.

summary: Ctesiphon, on the Tigris south-east of present-day Baghdad, was founded in the late 120s BCE and served as the royal capital of the Parthians and Sasanians. The Arabs occupied it in 637, and it was depopulated by the end of the 8th century after Baghdad was founded.
references: Beate Dignas, Rome and Persia in Late Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
